answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1729–1797 · Anglo-Irish statesman, orator and political thinker
answer.sourceLine: Burke wrote the sentence in <cite>Reflections on the Revolution in France</cite>, published in November 1790. It sits inside his argument that the English constitution reconciles a fixed hereditary rule with a power of change in an emergency, and the sentence immediately after it warns that without such means a state “might even risk the loss of that part of the Constitution which it wished the most religiously to preserve.” We confirmed the wording in two independent transcriptions of the text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Reflections on the Revolution in France
A letter to the French aristocrat Charles-Jean-François Depont — the text opens “Dear Sir”
<cite>The Works of the Right Honourable Edmund Burke</cite>, vol. 3 (Project Gutenberg ebook 15679), and Wikisource

source.excerpt: … It is far from impossible to reconcile, if we do not suffer ourselves to be entangled in the mazes of metaphysic sophistry, the use both of a fixed rule and an occasional deviation, — the sacredness of an hereditary principle of succession in our government with a power of change in its application in cases of extreme emergency. … A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. Without such means it might even risk the loss of that part of the Constitution which it wished the most religiously to preserve. The two principles of conservation and correction operated strongly at the two critical periods of the Restoration and Revolution, when England found itself without a king. …
trail: The sentence appears in Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790). We read it in the text of Burke’s collected Works, vol. 3, at Project Gutenberg ↗, where it stands in the discussion of hereditary succession and the power of change.
A second, independent transcription carries exactly the same wording: Wikisource’s text of the Reflections ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), which matches where we found it in the primary text.

The work’s origin and publication date are given by Wikipedia’s article on the Reflections ↗: Burke wrote it as the second and longer of two replies to the French aristocrat Charles-Jean-François Depont, drafting it after he read Richard Price’s A Discourse on the Love of Our Country in January 1790. It was published in November 1790.

author.bio: Edmund Burke was an Anglo-Irish politician and philosopher who sat for many years in the British House of Commons as a Whig. He championed liberal causes, sided with the American colonists, and spent years pressing the impeachment of the governor-general of British India for corruption — which is why the ferocity of his Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) surprised allies and opponents alike. The same book made him the writer modern conservatism claims as its founding voice.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Burke wrote the Reflections as a letter. After the fall of the Bastille the French aristocrat Charles-Jean-François Depont asked what he made of the Revolution; Burke sent two replies, and the longer second one — drafted after he read Richard Price’s A Discourse on the Love of Our Country in January 1790 — became the book. It sold thirteen thousand copies in its first five weeks ↗.

His argument was never that change is wrong. The sentence sits inside a claim that England had twice saved its institutions — at the Restoration and at the Revolution — by repairing the damaged part rather than demolishing the whole. Coming from a man who had sided with the American colonists and spent years impeaching a governor-general of British India for corruption, the book surprised allies and opponents alike; it is also the text modern conservatism claims as its founding voice.
